 Mexican Surveillance Records Show Dengue and COVID-19 Lack Predictive Coupling
 by 
 November 12, 2026 
 in 
 Health 
 Reading Time: 7 mins read
 0 
 Mexican Surveillance Records Show Dengue and COVID-19 Lack Predictive Coupling
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 A comprehensive nationwide ecological time-series analysis examining disease surveillance data across Mexico has established that reported fluctuations in COVID-19 cases do not provide meaningful or stable predictive information regarding dengue transmission. Published in Discover Public Health, the study investigated whether national surveillance trajectories of the pandemic respiratory pathogen could explain, anticipate, or enhance statistical forecasts of weekly dengue case counts between January 2020 and May 2025. During the initial global expansion of SARS-CoV-2, substantial disruptions to human movement, healthcare operations, clinical diagnosis, and vector management generated widespread questions concerning how the two major public health threats might interact across shared populations. By examining longitudinal public health notification archives encompassing over one million dengue notifications and twenty million COVID-19 reports, the research group demonstrated that widely cited national inverse associations between the conditions represent statistical artifacts of broad calendar timing, divergent epidemic phases, and established seasonal cycles rather than biologically or epidemiologically coupled interactions.
 To evaluate potential connections across the federal health infrastructure, the investigators compiled paired weekly panels aggregated at the state level across all thirty-two Mexican federal entities. The observational dataset brought together 1,085,869 individual dengue notification records spanning from January 1, 2020, to May 24, 2025, alongside 20,632,470 surveillance reports documenting confirmed COVID-19 cases from January 1, 2020, to June 2, 2025. The researchers designated the federal-entity-week as their fundamental analytical unit, assigning notifications according to the patient’s state of official residence and the precise epidemiological week when clinical symptoms first emerged. Prioritizing symptom onset rather than administrative registration or centralized database upload dates allowed the epidemiological curves to reflect the biological timing of infection more faithfully. Because the investigation relied strictly on aggregated regional surveillance registers rather than individual clinical follow-ups, the authors emphasized that their conclusions specifically characterize macroscopic population surveillance trajectories and do not evaluate personal immunological interference, antibody cross-reactivity, or patient-level clinical risk.
 A critical technical step preceding inferential evaluation involved an exhaustive audit of daily symptom-onset reporting continuity to prevent structural gaps from skewing statistical estimations. In routine public health registries, calendar intervals characterized by absent data extracts can easily be misread by computational algorithms as true zero-transmission weeks, creating artificial drops in disease prevalence. The research team audited daily national records and detected ten specific calendar weeks where one or more days lacked surveillance entries within the dengue database. These coverage deficits were clustered closely around year-end maintenance periods and administrative database snapshot transitions, including late December dates across 2020, 2021, and 2022, as well as multiple consecutive reporting weeks in December 2023 and December 2024. Rather than filling these administrative data absences with artificial zeros, the researchers treated them as missing intervals and excluded them from subsequent correlation, lag, and machine-learning assessments. This data audit left an analytical baseline of 8,695 complete state-week observations for rigorous mathematical evaluation.
 Descriptive profiling of the two aggregated surveillance populations highlighted pronounced distinctions in patient demographics and clinical severity markers. Within the descriptive database, the median age recorded among dengue patients was 26 years, whereas individuals registered in the COVID-19 database had a substantially higher median age of 36 years. Severe clinical outcomes necessitating hospitalization were documented in 17.37 percent of registered dengue cases, compared with 7.65 percent of COVID-19 notifications. Underlying metabolic conditions such as diabetes were reported with greater frequency among individuals diagnosed with COVID-19. The temporal sequencing of national caseloads also showed distinct epidemic epochs: national COVID-19 burden concentrated heavily across the early pandemic interval between 2020 and 2022, which accounted for 92.9 percent of all COVID-19 entries, culminating in a single-week national peak of 668,175 notifications on January 10, 2022. Conversely, dengue transmission was predominantly concentrated in 2023 and 2024, representing 76.3 percent of total dengue records, reaching its maximum national weekly count of 28,210 cases on September 16, 2024.
 Geographical distribution across Mexico revealed marked contrasts between absolute caseload volumes and population-adjusted surveillance intensities. In unadjusted aggregate figures, gross dengue records predominated within populous, climatically receptive states including Jalisco, Veracruz, Guerrero, Morelos, and Oaxaca, whereas COVID-19 notification totals were overwhelmingly concentrated within Mexico City and the surrounding State of Mexico. To account for demographic scale, the authors carried out sensitivity analyses standardizing counts by fixed state population estimates from the 2020 INEGI Population and Housing Census, calculating notifications per 100,000 residents before log-transforming the figures. On this population-standardized scale, the highest cumulative dengue burdens emerged within Colima, Morelos, Nayarit, Yucatan, and Quintana Roo. In contrast, cumulative population-standardized COVID-19 notification rates achieved their greatest magnitudes in Mexico City, Baja California Sur, Tabasco, San Luis Potosi, and Colima, illustrating that geographical risk patterns operated under independent spatial and demographic influences.
 When examining unadjusted contemporaneous relationships across the entire five-year observation window, initial statistical measurements suggested an inverse correlation between the two diseases. Across the audited panel of 8,695 state-week points, log-transformed counts yielded a pooled Pearson correlation coefficient of -0.331 with a bootstrap 95 percent confidence interval spanning from -0.349 to -0.312, accompanied by a Spearman rank correlation coefficient of -0.311. Under population standardization, this inverse linear association shifted slightly to -0.386. Unadjusted state-level Pearson correlation coefficients across all 32 federal entities were likewise negative, showing a median value of -0.527. However, when the authors stratified the data across individual calendar years, this apparent nationwide relationship proved unstable. Annual Pearson correlation coefficients fluctuated erratically, registering at 0.020 in 2020, rising to a positive 0.096 in 2021, reversing to -0.102 in 2022, deepening to -0.312 in 2023, and moderating to -0.131 in 2024 and -0.170 during early 2025.
 To evaluate whether this pooled negative correlation reflected genuine biological displacement or mere shared temporal architecture, the researchers applied systematic statistical controls removing spatial and calendar structures. When simple state fixed effects were extracted from the count-scale panel, the pooled negative correlation sharpened to -0.509, indicating that baseline geographical variation was not the primary driver of the inverse association. However, isolating and removing calendar-week mean effects caused the correlation to collapse to -0.035. Simultaneously eliminating both state fixed effects and calendar-week variations reduced the pooled coefficient to -0.049. A parallel two-way residualization conducted on the population-standardized panel yielded an equally negligible correlation of -0.052. These diagnostic steps proved that the perceived negative relationship observed across national registries was heavily driven by broad seasonal timing and multi-year shifts in pandemic waves rather than an inherent inhibitory relationship between the circulating pathogens.
 The research team extended this evaluation by fitting state-specific flexible models to separate residual disease variation from recurrent seasonal rhythms and continuous secular trends. Within each federal entity, log-transformed case series were adjusted using categorical indicators for calendar year, a cyclic cubic spline with six degrees of freedom across epidemiological weeks, and a cubic regression spline with twelve degrees of freedom representing continuous nonlinear time. Following this rigorous detrending process, the pooled residual Pearson correlation dropped to -0.055, and the Spearman rank correlation fell to -0.052. When evaluated across individual jurisdictions, state-specific adjusted Pearson correlations displayed a median of -0.062, spanning from -0.267 to +0.238. Crucially, only nine of the thirty-two federal entities maintained statistically significant associations following Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate corrections, and these retained estimates showed conflicting positive and negative signs, confirming that consistent nationwide coupling was entirely absent.
 Temporal alignment was further interrogated through rolling cross-correlation profiles spanning lead and lag windows from minus twelve weeks to plus twelve weeks, using exact calendar dates to prevent missing intervals from bridging artificially. In unadjusted analyses, raw cross-correlations remained broadly negative across the entire twenty-four-week window, reaching their strongest inverse point at lag zero rather than displaying a distinct leading offset. Once the series were adjusted for state-specific year, cyclic week, and nonlinear time components, the lag structure became markedly attenuated, leaving a peak correlation of only -0.114 at a two-week lag and an adjusted contemporaneous value of -0.055. Applying fourth-order autoregressive prewhitening to remove intrinsic serial dependency within each residual series completely extinguished the remaining signal, yielding a maximum absolute Pearson correlation of merely 0.053 at lag zero. Concordance between high-burden epidemic peaks was similarly disjointed; only five states exhibited dengue and COVID-19 surges occurring within two weeks of each other, while the median temporal distance separating peak burdens was 23 weeks.
 The decisive methodological test of whether COVID-19 surveillance metrics provide actionable utility for dengue early-warning systems was conducted via a formal out-of-sample predictive ablation experiment. Using regularized ElasticNetCV regression architectures, the researchers established an autoregressive dengue baseline incorporating historic dengue lags from one to four weeks, categorical epidemiological week indicators, and state effects. An augmented comparator model incorporated this identical baseline while adding contemporaneous COVID-19 metrics alongside twelve historical weekly COVID-19 lags. Both models were trained and tested against an identical holdout evaluation block encompassing the final 20 percent of calendar weeks starting on April 22, 2024, comprising 1,278 complete state-week observations. The baseline dengue model achieved high predictive accuracy, yielding a root mean squared error on the log10 scale of 0.1753 and an R-squared value of 0.9597, closely aligned with a naive single-week autoregressive benchmark that attained a root mean squared error of 0.1782.
 Incorporating the extensive suite of contemporaneous and lagged COVID-19 surveillance predictors produced virtually no change in forecast performance, shifting the test root mean squared error to 0.1749 and the R-squared value to 0.9599. This absolute root mean squared error reduction of 0.0004 represented an improvement of just 0.23 percent, accompanied by an incremental R-squared gain of only 0.00019. Paired block bootstrap resampling across two thousand test-week replications yielded an uncertainty interval spanning from -0.0019 to +0.0011 for root mean squared error and -0.00052 to +0.00086 for R-squared, both broadly encompassing zero and confirming that the negligible difference lacked statistical reliability. Furthermore, predictive contributions behaved inconsistently across time and seasonal strata: incorporating COVID-19 lags slightly reduced error in 2024 evaluations but actively worsened predictions during 2025, while showing marginal error reductions within high dengue transmission seasons that reversed into degraded performance outside those empirical seasonal windows.
 In evaluating the broader relevance of their findings, the authors detailed several methodological constraints inherent to the surveillance dataset. Foremost among these limitations was the absence of harmonized pre-2020 historical dengue observations within the analyzed records, which prevented the construction of a pre-pandemic counterfactual baseline to isolate normal multi-year cyclic swings and viral serotype replacements from pandemic-induced operational disruptions. Furthermore, local climatic drivers, ambient temperature, precipitation, humidity, and direct entomological indices were not integrated into the statistical panel, meaning unmeasured environmental forcing could explain residual variations. While the automated data audit successfully identified ten incomplete calendar weeks, it could not reconstruct unnotified infections or measure subtle diagnostic delays. Despite these factors, the investigation established that public health forecasting frameworks must rely directly on dengue’s intrinsic autoregressive momentum, environmental determinants, vector control operations, and seasonal structures rather than treating COVID-19 case series as predictive indicators.
 Subject of Research: Ecological time-series analysis of dengue and COVID-19 surveillance dynamics in Mexico
 Article Title: A nationwide ecological time-series analysis found no stable temporal or predictive relationship between dengue and COVID-19 surveillance records in Mexico from 2020 to 2025
 Article References: Garcia-Atutxa, I., Cruz-Herrero, C. L., & Villanueva-Flores, F. (2026). A nationwide ecological time-series analysis found no stable temporal or predictive relationship between dengue and COVID-19 surveillance records in Mexico from 2020 to 2025.
